bib.title: SWIFTSAGE: A Generative Agent with Fast and Slow Thinking for Complex Interactive Tasks
bib.venue: NeurIPS 2023 (37th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems)

read.skipped: References skimmed only; figures not viewed (captions from text)

question: Can an agent that combines a small fine-tuned LM (fast) with prompted LLM planning (slow) solve complex interactive tasks more effectively and cheaply than per-step LLM prompting agents?
hypothesis: Integrating behavior cloning (System 1) and LLM planning-and-grounding (System 2) via a switching heuristic gives better performance and efficiency than either alone or than SayCan/ReAct/Reflexion.
contributions: SWIFTSAGE dual-process agent framework (SWIFT + SAGE modules)
Heuristic to switch between modules with an action buffer
State-of-the-art on 30 ScienceWorld task types with fewer tokens per action

method.summary: SWIFT is a flan-t5-large (770m) fine-tuned by behavior cloning on oracle ScienceWorld trajectories and acts by default. When stuck, invalid, critical or an exception appears, SAGE prompts GPT-4 once for plan answers (Q1-Q5) and once to ground the next subgoal into an action buffer of several actions; control returns to SWIFT when the buffer empties.

training.steps: 500 steps, selected based on dev loss

inference.samples: one round per task variation (Reflexion up to four rounds); number of runs/seeds not stated
inference.prompting: SAGE: one planning prompt answering Q1-Q5, then a grounding prompt with formal action templates, recent 10 steps and plan answers; in-context demos of full trajectories of one or two training variations per task type for baselines

parameters.switch_other: invalid action, critical decision (focus on), unexpected observation
parameters.buffer_halt: two consecutive invalid or exception actions revert to SWIFT

other.saycan_ranking: SentenceBERT over valid actions vs top 5 generations
other.react_reflexion: best single generation, valid action with minimal edit distance

metrics.name: tokens per action (tpa)

eval.protocol: 270 test variations; no seeds or significance tests stated; Reflexion gets up to 4 rounds vs 1 for others

prompts.text:
▶Q1(locate objects): “To complete the task, which objects do I need to collect? Please list them and their possible locations one by one.”
▶Q2(track objects): “Are there any objects that have not been collected yet?”
▶Q3(plan subgoals): “To complete the task most efficiently, what are the important subgoals to achieve? Please list the subgoals one by one.”
▶Q4(track progress): “Considering these subgoals, what have I already completed? And which subgoal should I focus on right now?”
▶Q5(handle exceptions): “Have I made any mistakes that might prevent me from efficiently completing the next subgoal? If any , how should I fix them?”

limits: Evaluated only on ScienceWorld, a textual simulator with a limited action set (authors concede).
No safeguards against hazardous real-world actions.
SAGE depends on closed LLMs (GPT-4); scalability and cost concern; open-source LLMs have shorter input limits.
Switching is a hand-written heuristic; authors say a learned switch is future work.
Reflexion given up to four rounds vs one for others, so comparison is not fair (authors say so).
Baselines require human subgoal annotations (ReAct/Reflexion); SwiftSage does not.
No seeds, variance or significance tests; ablations are small-scale and not tabulated.
SWIFT trained on oracle (shortest correct) trajectories, so it cannot learn to fix mistakes and repeats actions on exceptions.
